What real DJs do, from the data¶

A study of real DJ sets: which tracks DJs play, how they move from one to the next, and how much they repeat themselves. Every number comes from published tracklists or from measurements on the audio of the mixes. How the measuring was done, and how far to trust each number, is in the appendix.

1. The data¶

Real DJ sets, from published tracklists and from the audio of the mixes themselves. For every set we know the DJ, the genre, and whether it was a club or festival set or a radio show or podcast. For a part of them the audio of every track and its exact place in the mix was known, and every transition in those sets was cut out and measured: when each sound comes in and goes out, when the bass swaps, how long two tracks play together. Where the sets came from is in the appendix.

Count
DJs 459
Mixes 3,892
Transitions listed in tracklists 51,269
Transitions measured on the audio 6,731
Distinct tracks 41,763
Hours of mix audio measured 1,559
Years 2014 to 2026

2. What DJs play¶

DJs do not share their tracks. We counted every track in 3,876 sets. Nine tracks in ten were played by a single DJ, and eight in ten appeared in one set only. One track in the whole collection was played by ten or more DJs. There is no playlist that the DJs of a genre all play from.

Where tracks are shared, it is between two DJs, not across a genre. When a track is played by more than one DJ, it is usually because two particular DJs play a lot of the same music. Amelie Lens and Charlotte de Witte have 89 tracks in common, Aly & Fila and Paul van Dyk 89, Chris Lake and FISHER 66. Take two DJs of the same genre at random and they share about ten.

The most played tracks of each genre. The twenty tracks that appear in the most sets, with how many DJs play them. Where one DJ has many sets in the data, the list is that DJ's repertoire, and the DJ count beside each track says so.

3. How DJs build a set¶

In a club, DJs play tracks they have played before. On radio they play new ones. In club and festival sets, four plays in ten are tracks the DJ had already played in an earlier set. In radio shows and podcasts it is one play in ten. Ben Böhmer, RÜFÜS DU SOL and Anyma repeat seven club plays in ten. Claptone, Scuba and Noisia almost never play a track twice.

Most tracks stay in DJ sets for a few months only. Of the tracks that were played more than once, four in ten were never played again after three months. One in six was still being played two years later. Trance and drum and bass keep tracks the longest.

4. Tempo¶

Techno is played faster every year. In 2016 techno sets ran at 126 beats per minute. In 2026 they run at 145, a step up almost every year in between. No other genre has moved like that.

DJs change the speed of the tracks they play. Half of all plays run more than one percent faster or slower than the track's own tempo, and faster is more common than slower. Techno DJs change the speed most, afro house DJs least.

5. The DJs¶

Some DJs mostly play their own music. Chase & Status fill 57 of every 100 plays with their own tracks, Anyma 47, Pendulum 46, FISHER 30. Carl Cox plays his own tracks 4 times in 100, Solomun 3.

The artists a DJ plays show their taste. For every play we looked up how many people listen to that artist on Last.fm. Amelie Lens fills four plays in ten with artists under ten thousand listeners. Fred again.. plays almost only his own tracks, so 98 plays in 100 are an artist with over a million listeners. The listener counts are still being fetched, and each row says how many plays they cover.

6. The cast's tracks¶

For each DJ of the cast, the tracks they have played in more than one set, with a link where the data has one, and the tracks that no other DJ in the collection plays. A DJ who plays almost every track once has no favourites, and the page says so.

7. How they mix¶

The transitions, measured on the audio of 7,600 changes from one track to the next. The cards explain each kind of transition the mixer knows, the grid shows which kind each DJ uses most, and the dots show how long two tracks play at the same time. The genre explains almost none of it; the DJ does.
